title: German Occupation Administration Takes Shape
subtitle: From military conquest to civilian rule
body:
A government for conquest

The administrative change of 26 October 1939 turned Germany’s conquest of Poland into a differentiated system of rule. Western and northern territories were incorporated into the Reich, while Hans Frank assumed civilian authority over the separate General Government. The distinction assigned different institutions and purposes to the conquered territory, affecting law, property, work and settlement. Administrators, police and economic agencies now acquired continuing powers over the inhabitants: defeat was translated into rules about residence, property and work, enforced through institutions that people would encounter repeatedly. Understanding that process requires examining both the formal powers granted in decrees and the overlapping institutions that exercised them. [1] The [28 September treaty](/articles/german-soviet-boundary-treaty-1939-09-28) allocated the occupiers’ spheres; the October measures specified how Germany would govern its share. Economic exploitation and racial transformation were central to the assignment, but they did not always generate compatible demands. Removal of a population could deprive an enterprise of workers, while an area designated to receive deportees still required food, transport and services. These tensions help explain the emerging administration’s uneven priorities. Its institutional divisions reflected the regime’s attempt to pursue several coercive purposes at once, with different agencies asserting authority over the same resources and people. [2] [3] Three decrees supplied the framework. Hitler’s 7 October decree on strengthening German nationhood—*Festigung deutschen Volkstums*—gave Heinrich Himmler responsibility for bringing ethnic Germans into the Reich’s orbit, establishing settlements, and eliminating the influence of populations defined as threatening to German interests. The decree combined resettlement with coercion from its inception: Himmler could take general and administrative measures to carry out that racial programme. Its categories expressed Nazi ideology, not objective differences in people’s entitlement to live in their own country. [4] The decree dated 8 October, *über Gliederung und Verwaltung der Ostgebiete*, concerned the organisation and administration of the eastern territories to be incorporated into Germany. The decree dated 12 October, *über die Verwaltung der besetzten polnischen Gebiete*, addressed the occupied Polish territories outside those annexations. Its first sections placed that remainder under a governor general, appointed Frank, and made him directly subordinate to Hitler. 26 October was the effective administrative changeover, rather than the date on which all three instruments had been issued. The annexation decree initially specified 1 November; a further decree of 20 October advanced its operation to 26 October. [5] [6]

Synchronising the occupation

An effective date brought forward

The annexation decree initially specified 1 November 1939. A further decree on 20 October advanced its operation to 26 October, bringing it into line with the General Government’s administrative changeover. Pospieszalski identifies both the amendment and the need to avoid leaving the incorporated territories under military administration after the neighbouring civilian system had begun. The adjustment reveals coordination between legal instruments that a single anniversary date tends to conceal.

[5]

Reading the legal record

A date on a decree is not always its full history

Legal historian Karol Marian Pospieszalski argued, from Frank’s recollections and the surrounding decisions, that the decree bearing the date 12 October was actually signed later, probably around 19 October. That is a reconstruction of its preparation, distinct from the date printed on the instrument. Its effective date, 26 October, remains the relevant administrative turning point here. The distinction illustrates why publication, signature and implementation should not automatically be treated as a single event.

[5]

Choosing the territory—and changing its population

The annexed lands did not form one uniform province. The October settlement created Reichsgaue, territorial units combining state administration with Nazi Party power, at West Prussia and Posen. The former became Danzig–West Prussia on 2 November; the latter received the name Wartheland on 29 January 1940. Those familiar later names can obscure the sequence. Posen, centred on Poznań, was governed by Arthur Greiser; Albert Forster headed the northern unit, which brought together the former Free City of Danzig, much of Polish Pomerania and the Corridor, and territory previously administered within German East Prussia. [7] Danzig requires a qualification. Before the war, it was a Free City under League of Nations protection, with specified Polish rights; it was not simply another province of the Polish Republic. German incorporation of Danzig and annexation of sovereign Polish territory were therefore distinct acts, even when the occupation subsequently placed them within the same administrative unit. Elsewhere, Germany enlarged existing provinces. The Ciechanów region went into East Prussia, while Polish Upper Silesia, including Katowice, was attached to Silesia. Describing every annexed district as part of either Posen or Danzig–West Prussia would erase these important differences. [8] [1] Łódź illustrates how unsettled the boundary initially remained. The city’s incorporation followed in November, with 9 November identified in the administrative chronology, rather than being a completed fact of 26 October. Nor should its later German name, Litzmannstadt, be projected backward: that renaming occurred in 1940. What would become the Wartheland consequently included substantial territory beyond Germany’s pre-1914 frontier. German annexation extended well beyond an attempt to restore Germany’s borders before the Treaty of Versailles. It expanded the Reich into areas whose Polish population and institutions the occupiers then intended to subordinate or displace. [7] [9] [10] The German division also did not encompass every territorial adjustment arising from the invasion. Slovakia had participated in the September attack, but its formal agreement with Germany transferring disputed Polish border districts was signed on **21 November**. That later act should not be folded into the German administrative settlement of 26 October. It belonged to a separate bilateral arrangement involving Spisz and Orawa, regions where border disputes had preceded the war. Distinguishing the agreements identifies which government asserted authority, over which places, and at what stage. [11] The economic attraction was substantial. These annexations took in important agricultural and industrial regions; Upper Silesia brought industrial capacity, while the western territories offered productive farmland. Göring’s instructions of 19 October made the intended distinction explicit: areas incorporated into Germany were to have their productive resources preserved and developed within the German economy. The General Government was to surrender raw materials, machinery, and enterprises useful to the German war effort. Territory, population, and economic assets were being assigned different purposes within the same project of domination. [10] [3] Racial policy gave annexation a demographic purpose. Himmler’s mandate treated resettlement and the assignment of new living areas as tasks of state, subordinating existing residence and Polish citizenship to categories defined by the regime. The aim was to transform the population, rather than simply recognise an existing territorial condition. Benefits offered to arriving ethnic Germans were consequently connected to the removal and dispossession of other inhabitants. Although later procedures and the scale of deportation were still developing, the link between settlement and coercion was already embedded in the authority granted on 7 October. [4] This also helps explain why Germany did not annex everything it occupied. In the record of Hitler’s 17 October conference with Wilhelm Keitel, the remaining Polish territory was assigned a low standard of living, a supply of labor, and a military role. Roads, railways, and communications were to remain useful to Germany, while the emergence of an independent Polish leadership was to be prevented. The area would also receive people removed from the Reich. Keeping it outside direct incorporation allowed the regime to exploit and police its inhabitants without undertaking to absorb them into the national community it claimed to be constructing. This was a deliberate allocation of functions, although particular borders and practices remained subject to argument. [2]

Frank’s authority, and its limits

The General Government began with four districts: Kraków, Warsaw, Radom, and Lublin. Galicia was added only in 1941. Frank, a lawyer and longstanding Nazi, presided over an administration in which German district heads and subordinate officials exercised authority over occupied communities. The 26 October organisational ordinance designated Kraków as his official seat. This was a German governmental decision, not a transfer of the Polish Republic’s capital: Warsaw’s reduced place in the occupation hierarchy did not make it cease to be Poland’s capital in Polish political life. [1] [6] The choice of Kraków also illustrates how administrative designation preceded practical consolidation. Frank initially worked from Łódź, whose impending incorporation into the Reich made it an unsuitable permanent seat for the separate General Government. His official move to Kraków followed in early November. Reading the ordinance alongside this sequence reveals a government being assembled amid continuing territorial decisions. Its founding date marks a transfer of authority, while the location and operation of its offices remained matters to be implemented. [5] The founding decree conferred extensive authority on Frank, but also contained the seeds of competing claims. He answered directly to Hitler and was assigned all branches of administration. Yet the Council of Ministers for the Defence of the Reich and Göring, as plenipotentiary for the Four-Year Plan, could also legislate for the territory. Reich authorities retained powers connected with wider German economic planning; the finance minister had to approve Frank’s budget, and the occupied territory itself was to bear the costs of administration. Frank’s government thus possessed a separate administrative identity without acquiring sovereign independence. Its inhabitants were expected to finance the machinery imposed on them. [6] Police authority created overlapping chains of command. Frank’s security ordinance of 26 October made the Higher SS and Police Leader responsible to him on matters of fundamental importance, while permitting independent action and police regulations in other areas. The SS hierarchy also connected that official to Himmler. This distribution of powers complicated civilian control without making Frank an opponent of repression: his own ordinance authorised the coercive machinery. Jurisdictional conflict must therefore be examined as a feature of the occupation’s operation, rather than as evidence that its administrators stood outside the system’s violence. [6] [12] The army’s withdrawal from general administration did not signify the end of military interests or a transition from violence to restraint. Hitler’s 17 October conference explicitly preserved the territory’s strategic importance, including the maintenance of communications for military use. The same record instructed the administration to prevent Polish political consolidation and denied that familiar legal restrictions should impede its racial objectives. Here the contrast with Hitler’s 6 October public speech is especially revealing. Before the Reichstag he had advertised peace, restored economic life, and the possible formation of a restricted Polish state; in the internal discussion, subsistence, labor extraction, and the suppression of leadership defined the assignment. [2] [13] References to a residual Polish state reveal the distance between political language and the institutions created. Hitler raised the possibility publicly, and the 17 October record employed the term independence while denying the population independent political organisation. Neither statement established a Polish government. The authority actually created answered to the German leadership, which retained the power to revise its boundaries and functions. Its future remained open to decisions from above while its inhabitants lacked an authorised means to determine that future themselves. [13] [2]

Occupation at the counter, the workplace, and the school

The new order did not abolish every existing institution. Section 4 of the 12 October decree retained existing law insofar as it did not contradict Germany’s assumption of administration. That condition was decisive. Continuity served the occupier’s convenience and could be withdrawn when German policy required it. On 26 October, a separate ordinance provided for both German and Polish jurisdictions, reserving to German courts the protection of German security, prestige, persons, and property. Polish courts were therefore permitted a subordinate role rather than recognised as the judicial authority of an independent state. Detailed arrangements continued to follow; the whole later court system should not be imagined as complete on its first day. [6] The preservation of selected municipal functions followed the same logic. Local records, finances and services required personnel and administrative continuity; the ordinance of 28 November subsequently made mayors accountable to occupation authorities who controlled appointment and supervision. A Polish official’s continued presence could therefore conceal a fundamental change in the authority exercised through the office. Assessing individual conduct requires further distinctions between maintaining essential services, responding to coercion and assisting persecution. The institution’s subordination establishes the setting in which those actions occurred, without determining every official’s motives or behaviour. [6] One of Frank’s first measures reached directly into personal identity. The 26 October *Kennkarte* ordinance required identity cards for the Polish population of the General Government. They were to record name, birth and descent, marital status, occupation, religion, and state affiliation, and to include a fingerprint. Implementation was entrusted to the Higher SS and Police Leader. The order did not mean that every inhabitant received a new document that day. It did establish the administrative ambition: individuals would become legible to the occupation through a set of officially recorded characteristics, including characteristics the regime used to distribute privileges and impose persecution. [6] Labor regulations made unequal treatment explicit. The 26 October ordinance imposed a public labor obligation on Polish inhabitants aged eighteen to sixty, while providing separate rules for Jews. It specified agricultural work, public construction, transport infrastructure, and land improvement; people able to demonstrate continuing socially useful employment were not supposed to be called up under this particular obligation. Such qualifications did not make the system voluntary. They show how an administration could claim the power to allocate labor while distinguishing between those it considered already usefully employed and those it intended to direct elsewhere. [6] The parallel decree for Jews introduced compulsory labor and envisaged forced-labor groups, with implementation assigned to the SS and police leader. These were two differently organised mechanisms, issued on the same date. Polish Jews were citizens of the same republic, but Nazi administration separated them through racial categories and subjected them to additional persecution. Later measures widened the machinery: in December, district authorities received permission to extend the general Polish labor obligation to fourteen-to-eighteen-year-olds. That later extension should not be substituted for the original October age range. [6] Education reveals the same combination of practical dependence and political destruction. On 31 October, Frank ordered the reopening of Polish elementary and vocational schools while separating German and Polish pupils and teachers. Polish private schools required permission; the ordinance reserved higher educational institutions for further regulation. The policy allowed forms of schooling useful to a subordinated workforce while denying any general guarantee of autonomous intellectual life. It was followed on 6 November by the arrest of Kraków academics summoned to hear a German official’s address. That attack belongs to the weeks after the administrative changeover, but it demonstrates how little protection the appearance of civilian government offered to established Polish institutions. [6] [14] An ordinance of 26 October also subjected publication, printing and distribution to permission, covering periodical and non-periodical material. The requirement placed the means of public communication under an administration committed to preventing independent Polish political organisation. Its reach extended beyond newspapers to publishers, teachers, associations and religious activity that depended on printed material. Censorship thus operated through routine decisions about authorisation as well as through seizures and violence. The bureaucratic procedure supplied a continuing means to restrict national and communal life after the immediate military conquest. [6] [2]

Property, displacement, and terror

Göring’s 19 October economic instructions illuminate what administrative “order” meant for property. He demanded centralised custody of assets taken from Polish hands through the Main Trustee Office East, the *Haupttreuhandstelle Ost*, and described arrangements for state property and private Polish and Jewish property. The office could appoint administrators and replace ones installed by other agencies. Local confiscations were subject to confirmation. Göring condemned unauthorised seizures and private enrichment, but the purpose was to secure the proceeds for the Reich. Regulating confiscation did not restore the owners’ rights; it established which German institution should control what had been taken. [3] Göring’s instructions acknowledged that the newly divided territories had formed a connected economy, and claimed direction from Berlin despite their different administrative treatment. His demand to remove useful machinery from the General Government included a practical exception: where transfer would take too long, enterprises could fulfil German orders in place. The exception explains how preservation of production could accompany dispossession. It sustained output useful to the Reich without restoring the rights of the owners or workers. Economic continuity was therefore selective, determined by the occupier’s assessment of value and the constraints on extracting it. [3] Displacement was already more than a future program. In Gdynia, expulsions began in October, before the formal establishment of the General Government. Polish residents lost access to homes in a port the Germans intended to use for their own purposes. At the same time, ethnic Germans were arriving from the Baltic region: Monika Tomkiewicz’s account records arrivals at Gdańsk on 15 October and at Gdynia on 24 October. Not every arrival remained in the port, and the later settlement apparatus should not be read back into each early movement. Even so, removal and reception were already operating together, turning racial plans into demands for housing, transport, property, and administrative decisions. [15] [16] The formal changeover neither initiated nor ended terror. Einsatzgruppen, SS and police formations, military personnel and the ethnic German *Selbstschutz* took part in attacks on civilians, including potential sources of organised Polish leadership. Photographic records from around Bydgoszcz and Toruń identify particular settings and perpetrators, including murdered teachers near Fordon and prisoners guarded near Tuchola. Such evidence connects administrative objectives to the destruction of the people and institutions that might sustain independent social life. The establishment of civilian offices cannot be treated as a chronological boundary separating conquest from violence. [17] Anti-Jewish administration was developing through instructions that predated Frank’s government. On **21 September**, Reinhard Heydrich directed security-police commanders to concentrate Jewish populations in selected towns, favouring railway connections, and to establish Jewish councils whose members would be held responsible for carrying out German demands. Census-taking, accommodation and transport were made administrative tasks under coercion. Economic usefulness could delay removal: the instructions allowed enterprises needed for German purposes to keep operating temporarily. Such exceptions protected the occupier’s interests, not the owners’ rights. [18] These instructions should not be paraphrased as a universal order to establish sealed ghettos immediately. They set a direction of concentration and control while leaving implementation to develop unevenly. The first ghetto in occupied Poland was established at **Piotrków Trybunalski in October 1939**; other localities followed different timetables. Jewish councils, or *Judenräte*, were therefore emerging within a system of compulsory mediation: German authorities imposed responsibilities on community representatives while retaining coercive power over both representatives and those they were required to administer. The distinction between an instruction and its local execution helps explain why the same month could bring different restrictions to different towns. [19] [18] The autumn campaign against Polish elites, commonly associated with the *Intelligenzaktion*, must be distinguished from the AB-Aktion of spring 1940. Auschwitz was also a later development, not a camp already operating at this October changeover. For Jews, humiliation, forced labor, dispossession, and expulsion were already realities, but the later extermination system cannot be projected backward as an institution fully formed in 1939. The General Government’s general armband decree was issued on 23 November and took effect on 1 December, although local badge requirements had appeared earlier. These distinctions do not diminish the crimes already committed. They make it possible to identify the decisions through which persecution expanded. [20] [16] [21] [6]

A resident’s recollection

Covering the windows in Gdynia

Jadwiga Kocuniak later recalled sheltering with her family in a friend’s building on Świętojańska Street when German troops entered Gdynia. Soldiers shouted orders to cover the windows and not look out, threatening to shoot. Preserved in Monika Tomkiewicz’s account, the recollection concerns the occupation’s first days, before October’s administrative settlement. It conveys the immediate coercion behind the official language of restored order. [16]

Polish continuity under occupation

The division of administrative space intensified the dislocation created by defeat. Homes, workplaces and relatives could come under different authorities, while refugees encountered guarded routes, document requirements and arrest. Research on Jewish refugees records returns towards German-occupied homes prompted by exhaustion and the desire to rejoin family. These decisions reveal the constraints under which inhabitants sought safety: resources and information were limited, while occupation authorities controlled permission to move. Restoring those circumstances prevents later knowledge of persecution from being projected onto choices made within the uncertainty of autumn 1939. [22] Political continuity developed on a different plane. Władysław Raczkiewicz succeeded to the presidency, and General Władysław Sikorski headed the Polish government established in France. Their authority did not depend on recognition by the occupiers. In a 30 September communication to Washington, Ambassador Jerzy Potocki explicitly rejected the German–Soviet partition agreement as illegal and reaffirmed Poland’s intention to restore its territory and its people’s rights. The [previous study](/articles/german-soviet-boundary-treaty-1939-09-28#poland-refuses) examines that protest in its diplomatic setting. By 26 October, its relevance had become even more concrete: Germany was creating administrations over a country whose government continued to reject the premise on which they rested. [23] [24] Inside occupied Poland, organised resistance was also beginning to take institutional form. On 27 September, General Michał Tokarzewski-Karaszewicz began building *Służba Zwycięstwu Polski*, the Service for Poland’s Victory. The organisation represented an early attempt to sustain coordinated struggle after the collapse of open military defence. It was not yet the Home Army. Sikorski created the Union of Armed Struggle in November 1939; the Home Army name followed in 1942. Keeping these stages separate preserves something important about October: clandestine structures had to be built under conditions of uncertainty, surveillance, and repression, rather than simply continuing as an already complete underground state. [23]

Moscow’s parallel settlement, and the Western refusal

East of the partition line, the Soviet authorities were constructing a different justification for territorial absorption. Controlled elections on 22 October produced assemblies presented as expressions of popular will. The People’s Assembly of Western Ukraine met in Lviv from 26 October to 28; the Western Belorussian assembly met in Białystok later that month. German civilian administration and Soviet annexation therefore did not begin as identical legal acts on 26 October. Soviet incorporation proceeded through further decisions in November, with the USSR’s Supreme Soviet acting on Western Ukraine on 1 November and Western Belarus on 2 November. [25] [26] The Western Ukrainian assembly’s 27 October declaration proclaimed Soviet power and asserted unanimous popular consent. Read alongside the controlled electoral process, it records what the occupation wanted to claim, rather than demonstrating freely expressed agreement. Soviet consolidation also involved the NKVD and the persecution of people classified as enemies of the new order. Polish citizens of Jewish background could escape immediate exposure to Nazi racial persecution yet face Soviet attacks on private enterprise, religious and political institutions, or alleged “counterrevolutionary” activity. Their varied circumstances rule out treating either relief at German withdrawal or support from some individuals as consent on behalf of entire communities. [27] [28] Berlin and Moscow could cooperate without organising their territories in the same way. An American diplomatic report of 9 October recorded the arrival in Moscow of German economic negotiators, including representatives concerned with agriculture and railways, together with the head of the German frontier commission. This was the practical continuation of the settlement described in the earlier treaty study: frontiers, population arrangements, and economic cooperation all required implementation. The two governments shared an interest in consolidating their territorial gains and obstructing the return of independent Polish power. Their differing racial, social, and political programs nevertheless remained essential to understanding how each exercised control. [29] [24] Britain’s response challenged the political finality Germany sought. In the House of Commons on 12 October, Neville Chamberlain argued that Hitler’s proposals required acceptance of his conquests and his claimed freedom to deal with conquered peoples. Britain would not accept that foundation for peace. Chamberlain also cited Édouard Daladier’s 10 October broadcast, emphasising French agreement that fighting could not end without dependable security. France’s hosting of the Polish government gave that refusal a concrete institutional expression. Recognition, however, did not give either Western ally the immediate ability to dismantle the administrations being established inside Poland. Diplomatic continuity and the occupiers’ physical control existed simultaneously. [30] [23] The United States supplied a particularly clear statement of the distinction while remaining outside the war. On 2 October, Secretary of State Cordell Hull affirmed that seizure of territory did not extinguish a government’s legal existence and that American recognition of Poland continued. The statement is reproduced in a later American briefing paper, which should not be confused with a fresh declaration issued in 1945. Hull’s position did not prevent German officials from administering annexed districts or Frank from issuing decrees. It denied that those acts alone settled the international question of Poland’s existence. Germany had achieved control over territory without securing general acceptance of the political conclusion it drew from that control. [10]

The institutions of domination

The October settlement enlarged the institutional capacity for coercion while distributing authority among agencies with different jurisdictions. Annexation officials, Frank’s administration, police commanders and economic bodies could dispute priorities without releasing inhabitants from their combined demands. Production might be preserved while owners were dispossessed; elementary schooling might continue while autonomous intellectual life was attacked. The persistence of an office, factory or school consequently requires examination of whose purposes it now served and whose rights it could no longer protect. [3] [6] Decrees establish the powers claimed and procedures prescribed, but their implementation has to be reconstructed beside evidence of confiscation, expulsion and killing. Together, these records show how racial and political objectives became decisions about work, residence, education and property. The framework created in October enabled further measures without containing the whole later history of persecution in finished form. Precise chronology makes it possible to identify the subsequent choices through which coercion widened, and the institutions responsible for carrying them into effect. [17] [15] By late October, Poland’s recognised government operated abroad while resistance at home began to develop clandestine institutions. Recognition preserved a political claim but offered little immediate protection against the authorities controlling territory and daily life. German administration and Soviet incorporation proceeded through distinct institutions and ideological programmes, both overriding Polish independence. The collection’s sequence therefore ends with a transformation in the exercise of power: agreements made over Poland had acquired offices, regulations and coercive forces capable of reaching repeatedly into the lives of its inhabitants. [24] [10] [23]
author: R.G. Cruise
location: German-occupied Poland, with responses from Moscow and the Western capitals
summary: Annexation and the General Government gave German conquest different administrative forms. Decrees concerning property, labour, policing and local authority brought the occupiers’ power into daily life while the recognised Polish government continued abroad.

sourceMethod: Numbered citations lead to the sources below; each entry lists the passages cited and links back to its first use. The study uses contemporary decrees, diplomatic correspondence, the October 17 Hitler–Keitel conference record, and parliamentary proceedings alongside museum research and scholarly documentary history. Nazi and Soviet declarations are read as evidence of policy and official claims, not as proof of consent or legitimacy. The General Government documents were checked in the German transcriptions reproduced in Documenta Occupationis VI; the relevant printed pages are identified below. Selected sections of scholarly works were consulted, not the complete volumes. Daladier’s October 10 broadcast is accessed through Chamberlain’s October 12 parliamentary statement; Hull’s October 2 declaration through its reproduction in a 1945 American briefing paper. Measures in force on October 26 are distinguished from later implementation and subsequent decrees.
